text: Trust in the LORD with all thine heart; and lean not unto thine own understanding.
reflection: We like to understand things. We want to know why something happened, how it will turn out, and what we should do next. Understanding gives us a sense of control. But Proverbs points us to something deeper: "Trust in the LORD with all thine heart; and lean not unto thine own understanding." This does not mean we stop thinking. God gave us minds, and He expects us to use them. It means we do not lean our full weight on our own reasoning. Our understanding is limited. We see only a small part of the picture. God sees the whole. Leaning on our own understanding is like leaning on a cane that cannot hold us. Sooner or later, it gives way. Trusting God with all our heart means resting on Him even when we do not understand. This month we will think about trusting God in the storms of life. Begin today by handing Him the questions you cannot answer. Lean on Him instead.
question: What question you cannot answer could you hand to God today instead of leaning on your own understanding?
prayer: Lord, I trust You with all my heart and lean not on my own understanding. You see the whole picture when I see only a part. I lean on You today. Amen.

text: God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble.
reflection: Psalm 46 was written for a time of great upheaval. The psalmist imagines mountains crumbling into the sea, waters roaring, and nations in turmoil. Into that chaos, he declares, "God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble." A refuge is a place to run to for safety. Strength is the power to keep going. And a very present help means God is not far away when trouble comes. He is right here, readily available. Some help arrives too late. Some help is hard to reach. But God's help is near, immediate, and reliable. The psalmist does not say trouble will never come. He assumes it will. The earth may shake. But God remains a safe place and a source of strength. Whatever is shaking in your life right now, you can run to Him. He is not distant. He is present, right now, in the middle of it. Let Him be your refuge and your strength today.
question: What trouble are you facing today that you could run to God with first?
prayer: O God, You are my refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble. When everything around me shakes, I run to You. Be near me today. Amen.

text: Be still, and know that I am God: I will be exalted among the heathen, I will be exalted in the earth.
reflection: Later in the same psalm, after describing roaring waters and raging nations, God speaks directly: "Be still, and know that I am God." The words be still can also mean let go, stop striving, or cease fighting. It is an invitation to stop our frantic efforts and remember who is really in control. When storms come, our instinct is to do something, anything. We worry, plan, scramble, and try to fix things. Sometimes action is needed. But often what we need first is stillness. A quiet heart that remembers God is God, and we are not. He goes on to say, "I will be exalted among the heathen, I will be exalted in the earth." God's purposes will prevail. He will be honoured. Nothing that troubles you is beyond His reach. Today, take a few minutes to be still. Put down your phone, quiet your thoughts, and simply rest in the truth that He is God. Let that truth calm your heart.
question: Where could you stop striving today and spend a few quiet minutes remembering that God is God?
prayer: Lord, I choose to be still and know that You are God. Quiet my frantic striving, and let me rest in the truth that You are in control. Amen.

text: When thou passest through the waters, I will be with thee; and through the rivers, they shall not overflow thee: when thou walkest through the fire, thou shalt not be burned; neither shall the flame kindle upon thee.
reflection: God did not promise His people a life without waters and fires. He promised something better: His presence in them. "When thou passest through the waters, I will be with thee; and through the rivers, they shall not overflow thee: when thou walkest through the fire, thou shalt not be burned." Notice the word when, not if. Hard seasons are part of life. Floods rise and fires burn. Israel remembered walking through the Red Sea and crossing the Jordan River. Later, three young men would walk through a fiery furnace untouched. God had been with them every time. The promise is not that we will avoid difficulty, but that difficulty will not destroy us. The waters will not overwhelm us. The flames will not consume us. Why? Because He is with us. Whatever waters you are passing through today, you are not alone. The One who parted seas and walked in the fire walks with you.
question: What waters or fires are you passing through, and how does God's presence change how you face them?
prayer: Lord, You promised to be with me when I pass through the waters and the fire. I do not ask for an easy road, but I trust You to carry me through. Amen.

text: And he said unto them, Why are ye so fearful? how is it that ye have no faith?
reflection: The disciples were experienced fishermen. They knew the Sea of Galilee and its sudden storms. But this one was different. Waves crashed into the boat, and it began filling with water. Terrified, they woke Jesus, who was asleep on a cushion. He rose, rebuked the wind, and the sea became completely calm. Then He turned to them: "Why are ye so fearful? how is it that ye have no faith?" The question was not harsh but searching. They had seen Him heal the sick and cast out demons. Yet in the storm, fear took over. Jesus was in the boat with them the whole time. That is the point. Fear forgets who is present. Faith remembers. The storm was real, but so was the One sleeping in the stern. Whatever storm you are facing, Jesus is not absent. Let His question search your heart today. Then answer it with faith.
question: In the storm you are facing, what helps you remember that Jesus is in the boat with you?
prayer: Lord Jesus, You are in the boat with me, and the wind and the sea obey You. When fear rises in my storm, remind me that You are near. Amen.

text: But straightway Jesus spake unto them, saying, Be of good cheer; it is I; be not afraid.
reflection: It was the middle of the night, and the disciples were again struggling against wind and waves. Then they saw a figure walking toward them on the water. They cried out in fear, thinking it was a spirit. But Jesus called out, "Be of good cheer; it is I; be not afraid." Three short phrases, each one a gift. Be of good cheer: there is reason for courage. It is I: the One you know and trust is here. Be not afraid: fear does not have to rule you. Sometimes Jesus comes to us in ways we do not recognize at first. In the darkness and confusion, we may mistake His presence for something frightening. A trial we thought would destroy us turns out to be the very place He meets us. Listen for His voice in your storm today. He is saying, it is I. The One who walks on water is coming to you.
question: Could Jesus be coming to you in your storm in a way you have not yet recognized?
prayer: Lord Jesus, You say, be of good cheer; it is I; be not afraid. Open my eyes to recognize You in my storm today, and let Your voice calm my fear. Amen.

text: And immediately Jesus stretched forth his hand, and caught him, and said unto him, O thou of little faith, wherefore didst thou doubt?
reflection: After hearing Jesus' voice, Peter did something bold. He asked to come to Jesus on the water, and Jesus said, come. Peter stepped out of the boat and began to walk. But when he saw the wind, he became afraid and began to sink. He cried, Lord, save me. And "immediately Jesus stretched forth his hand, and caught him." Immediately. Jesus did not wait for Peter to go under. He did not let him struggle to prove a point. He reached out at once. Then He asked, "O thou of little faith, wherefore didst thou doubt?" Even this question came while Peter was safe in His grip. We all have moments when our faith falters. We start strong, then the wind catches our eye and we begin to sink. In those moments, call out to Him. His hand is quick to catch. Little faith is still faith, and a strong Saviour holds it.
question: Where do you feel yourself sinking, and could you call out to Jesus right now?
prayer: Lord Jesus, when I begin to sink, You reach out and catch me. Even when my faith falters, Your hand holds me. Save me, Lord, and hold me fast today. Amen.

text: What time I am afraid, I will trust in thee.
reflection: David wrote Psalm 56 when he was captured by the Philistines in Gath. He was alone, in enemy territory, and genuinely afraid. Out of that moment came this honest prayer: "What time I am afraid, I will trust in thee." David did not pretend to be fearless. He admitted that fear came. But he made a decision about what to do with it. Fear and trust are not always opposites that cannot exist together. Sometimes trust is the choice we make while we are still afraid. Courage is not the absence of fear. It is the decision to rely on God in the middle of it. This short verse is easy to memorize, and it is worth keeping close. When anxiety rises, when bad news comes, when you lie awake at night, you can repeat it. What time I am afraid, I will trust in thee. Say it today, and let it become your response whenever fear knocks.
question: What fear is present in you today, and how could you choose to trust God in the middle of it?
prayer: Lord, what time I am afraid, I will trust in You. I do not wait for fear to leave before I trust. I choose to trust You now, even while I am afraid. Amen.

text: Yea, though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil: for thou art with me; thy rod and thy staff they comfort me.
reflection: Psalm 23 begins in green pastures and beside still waters. But then the path turns dark: "Yea, though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil: for thou art with me." The Shepherd does not lead His sheep around every valley. Sometimes the path goes straight through. Valleys of grief, illness, loss, and uncertainty are part of life's journey. But notice two important words: walk through. The valley is not the destination. It is a passage. And we do not walk it alone. This is also the point in the psalm where David stops talking about the Shepherd and starts talking to Him. In the dark valley, the relationship becomes personal: thou art with me. The rod protects and the staff guides. If you are in a valley right now, take comfort. You are walking through it, not staying in it. And your Shepherd is right beside you every step.
question: What dark valley are you walking through, and how does the Shepherd's presence comfort you?
prayer: Lord, though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil, for You are with me. Walk with me through this dark place, my Shepherd. Amen.

text: He that dwelleth in the secret place of the most High shall abide under the shadow of the Almighty.
reflection: Have you ever stood in the shade on a scorching day? The relief is immediate. Psalm 91 uses that picture for life with God: "He that dwelleth in the secret place of the most High shall abide under the shadow of the Almighty." Dwelling and abiding are words of permanence. This is not about visiting God occasionally. It is about living close to Him, making His presence your home. The secret place suggests intimacy, a hidden refuge known to those who walk with Him. And the shadow of the Almighty speaks of protection. To be in someone's shadow, you must be very close to them. Psalm 91 goes on to describe dangers of every kind: snares, plagues, arrows, and terror by night. The promise is not that dangers vanish, but that those who stay close to God are sheltered. Today, do not just visit God. Dwell with Him. Stay close enough to remain in His shadow.
question: How could you stay close enough to God today to rest in His shadow?
prayer: Lord, I want to dwell in Your secret place, not just visit it. Keep me close enough to rest under Your shadow today, safe in Your presence. Amen.

text: I will say of the LORD, He is my refuge and my fortress: my God; in him will I trust.
reflection: After describing the shelter of God's presence, the psalmist makes it personal: "I will say of the LORD, He is my refuge and my fortress: my God; in him will I trust." Notice the word say. Faith is not only something we feel inside. It is something we declare. There is power in speaking truth aloud, especially when fear is loud. Notice also the word my, repeated again and again. My refuge. My fortress. My God. The psalmist does not speak of God as a distant idea or someone else's protector. He claims God as his own. A refuge is a place to run to. A fortress is a place that cannot be overrun. Together they paint a picture of total security. When you feel exposed, attacked, or overwhelmed, you have a place to go. Today, say it out loud. The Lord is my refuge and my fortress. My God, in Him will I trust. Let your words strengthen your faith.
question: What fear could you answer today by saying aloud that the Lord is your refuge?
prayer: Lord, You are my refuge and my fortress, my God, in You will I trust. When fear is loud, let me speak this truth and stand on it today. Amen.

text: The LORD is good, a strong hold in the day of trouble; and he knoweth them that trust in him.
reflection: The book of Nahum is mostly about judgment on the cruel city of Nineveh. But tucked into its opening chapter is a verse of great comfort: "The LORD is good, a strong hold in the day of trouble; and he knoweth them that trust in him." Even while describing God's power against evil, Nahum pauses to remind us of His goodness toward His people. God's strength is not something to fear if you are His. It is your protection. A stronghold was a fortified place on high ground where people fled when enemies attacked. In the day of trouble, God is that place. And the last line is tender: he knoweth them that trust in him. God does not merely tolerate those who trust Him. He knows them personally. He notices them, cares for them, and keeps track of them. In whatever trouble you face today, remember that God is good, He is strong, and He knows you by name.
question: What trouble could you bring to God today, knowing that He is good and knows you by name?
prayer: Lord, You are good, a stronghold in the day of trouble, and You know those who trust in You. Thank You that I am known by You. I trust You today. Amen.

text: He maketh the storm a calm, so that the waves thereof are still.
reflection: Psalm 107 tells stories of people in trouble who cried out to God and were rescued. One group were sailors caught in a terrible storm. The waves rose so high that their courage melted. They staggered like drunken men and were at their wits' end. Then they cried to the Lord, and "He maketh the storm a calm, so that the waves thereof are still." The same God who sends the wind can stop it. Storms do not have the final word. Many people reach a wits' end moment. Their own skill and strength run out. They have tried everything they know. That is often the moment when they finally cry out to God. And He hears. He may calm the storm around you, or He may calm the storm within you. Either way, His peace is real. If you are at your wits' end today, it is not the end. Cry out to Him. He can make the storm a calm.
question: Where are you at your wits' end, and could you cry out to God there?
prayer: Lord, when my strength runs out, You are still able. I cry out to You in my storm. Make the storm a calm, and bring me to the haven I need. Amen.

text: Fear thou not; for I am with thee: be not dismayed; for I am thy God: I will strengthen thee; yea, I will help thee; yea, I will uphold thee with the right hand of my righteousness.
reflection: This verse is like a series of hands reaching out to steady someone who is falling: "Fear thou not; for I am with thee: be not dismayed; for I am thy God." Then come three promises: "I will strengthen thee; yea, I will help thee; yea, I will uphold thee with the right hand of my righteousness." Every command not to fear is backed by a reason. Do not fear, because I am with you. Do not be dismayed, because I am your God. The reason we can let go of fear is not that the situation is easy. It is that God is present and God is ours. Then the promises build on one another. Strength for what we cannot do. Help for what we cannot manage. And upholding for when we cannot stand. The right hand was the hand of power. God's own hand holds you up. Read this verse slowly today. Let each phrase settle into your heart.
question: Which phrase of Isaiah 41:10 does your heart most need to hear today?
prayer: Lord, I will not fear, for You are with me. I will not be dismayed, for You are my God. Strengthen me, help me, and uphold me with Your right hand. Amen.

text: If it be so, our God whom we serve is able to deliver us from the burning fiery furnace, and he will deliver us out of thine hand, O king.
reflection: King Nebuchadnezzar set up a huge golden statue and commanded everyone to bow down to it. Three young Jewish men, Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, refused. Furious, the king threatened to throw them into a blazing furnace. Their reply was calm and confident: "our God whom we serve is able to deliver us from the burning fiery furnace, and he will deliver us out of thine hand, O king." They faced the most powerful ruler on earth, yet they spoke of a greater power. Our God is able. Those words have strengthened believers in every age. They did not know exactly how the story would end. But they knew who held their lives. Whatever threatens you today, whether a powerful person, a frightening diagnosis, or an impossible situation, God is able. His power is not limited by the size of the furnace. Stand on that truth today. Our God is able.
question: What are you facing today that you need to remember God is able to handle?
prayer: Lord, You are able to deliver. Whatever furnace I face today, help me trust Your power more than any threat around me. Amen.

text: But if not, be it known unto thee, O king, that we will not serve thy gods, nor worship the golden image which thou hast set up.
reflection: Yesterday we heard the bold confidence of three young men: God is able to deliver us. Today we hear what they said next, and it may be even more powerful: "But if not, be it known unto thee, O king, that we will not serve thy gods." They believed God could save them. But their faithfulness did not depend on Him doing so. Even if He chose not to rescue them from the fire, they would still refuse to bow. This is mature faith. It trusts God's power without demanding a specific outcome. It is not a faith that says, I will follow You if You give me what I want. It says, I will follow You no matter what. As it turned out, God did deliver them, walking with them in the flames. But their but if not is a model for us. Pray boldly for what you need. And settle in your heart that you will trust Him, even if not.
question: Is your trust in God tied to a particular outcome, and could you settle in your heart to trust Him even if not?
prayer: Lord, I believe You are able, and I ask You boldly. But even if You do not answer as I hope, I will still trust You and refuse to bow to anything else. Amen.

text: Yet I will rejoice in the LORD, I will joy in the God of my salvation.
reflection: The prophet Habakkuk ends his book with one of the most remarkable statements of faith in Scripture. He imagines the worst possible scenario for a farming nation: the fig tree without blossoms, no fruit on the vines, failed olive crops, empty fields, and no animals in the stalls. Total loss. And then he says, "Yet I will rejoice in the LORD, I will joy in the God of my salvation." Yet. That small word is enormous. Habakkuk's joy did not come from his circumstances. If it had, it would have vanished along with the crops. His joy came from God Himself, who does not change when the harvest fails. This kind of joy is not pretending everything is fine. It is choosing to rejoice in the One who remains when everything else is gone. What is failing in your life right now? Bring it honestly to God. Then, by faith, add Habakkuk's word: yet. Yet I will rejoice in the Lord.
question: What is failing in your life right now, and how could you still choose to rejoice in God today?
prayer: Lord, even if the fields fail and the stalls are empty, I will rejoice in You. Let my joy rest on who You are, not on what I have. Amen.

text: Though he slay me, yet will I trust in him: but I will maintain mine own ways before him.
reflection: Job lost his children, his wealth, and his health in a series of devastating blows. His friends came to comfort him but ended up accusing him of hidden sin. Job wrestled honestly with God, asking hard questions and voicing deep pain. Yet in the middle of his anguish, he made this declaration: "Though he slay me, yet will I trust in him." It is one of the strongest expressions of trust ever written. Job did not understand what God was doing. He could not see any reason for his suffering. But he refused to let go of God. His trust was not based on circumstances or explanations. It was anchored in who God is. Job's honesty is also a gift. He did not hide his questions. He brought them to God. Trust and honest questions can go together. If you are hurting and confused today, you can tell God exactly how you feel. And you can still choose, like Job, to hold on to Him.
question: What honest question could you bring to God today while still holding on to Him?
prayer: Lord, though I do not understand everything, I will trust in You. I bring You my honest questions, and I choose to hold on to You. Amen.

text: O our God, wilt thou not judge them? for we have no might against this great company that cometh against us; neither know we what to do: but our eyes are upon thee.
reflection: King Jehoshaphat received terrifying news. A vast army was marching against Judah. He had no military answer. So he gathered the people and prayed a prayer of total honesty: "we have no might against this great company that cometh against us; neither know we what to do: but our eyes are upon thee." It is a prayer anyone can pray. We have no power. We do not know what to do. But our eyes are on You. There is something freeing about admitting our limits. We do not have to pretend we have it all figured out. Jehoshaphat did not have a plan. He had a direction for his eyes. Where we look determines how we feel. If we stare only at the problem, fear grows. If we look to God, faith grows. The story ends with a great victory, but it began with a humble confession. If you do not know what to do today, pray this prayer. Fix your eyes on Him.
question: Where do you feel you have no power and no plan, and how could you fix your eyes on God there?
prayer: Lord, I do not know what to do, but my eyes are upon You. I admit my limits, and I look to You for the help I cannot give myself. Amen.

text: And he said, Hearken ye, all Judah, and ye inhabitants of Jerusalem, and thou king Jehoshaphat, Thus saith the LORD unto you, Be not afraid nor dismayed by reason of this great multitude; for the battle is not yours, but God's.
reflection: After King Jehoshaphat prayed, God answered through a prophet named Jahaziel. The message was clear: "Be not afraid nor dismayed by reason of this great multitude; for the battle is not yours, but God's." What a relief those words must have been. The army was still coming. The danger was still real. But the responsibility for the outcome had shifted. The battle belonged to God. The next day, Jehoshaphat sent singers ahead of the army, praising God. As they sang, God caused confusion among the enemy armies, and they defeated themselves. Judah did not have to lift a sword. Many of us carry battles as though everything depends on us. We lie awake strategizing and worrying. But some battles are simply not ours to fight. They belong to God. Our part is to trust, obey, and praise. What battle are you carrying today that you need to hand over? Let God fight it. Then lift your voice in praise.
question: What battle have you been carrying alone that you could hand over to God today?
prayer: Lord, the battle is not mine but Yours. I hand You the struggle I have been carrying, and I choose to praise You while You fight for me. Amen.

text: And Moses said unto the people, Fear ye not, stand still, and see the salvation of the LORD, which he will shew to you to day: for the Egyptians whom ye have seen to day, ye shall see them again no more for ever.
reflection: The Israelites had just left Egypt when they found themselves trapped. The Red Sea was in front of them, and Pharaoh's chariots were thundering behind. They panicked and accused Moses of leading them out to die. Moses answered, "Fear ye not, stand still, and see the salvation of the LORD, which he will shew to you to day." Stand still. In a moment that seemed to demand frantic action, God's first instruction was to stop, stop panicking and stop running. Then God would act. And He did. The sea parted, and they walked through on dry ground. Sometimes we feel trapped between impossible choices. Every direction looks hopeless. In those moments, panic tells us to do something, anything. But faith sometimes says, be still and watch God work. He has ways of escape we cannot imagine. If you feel trapped today, take a breath. Stand still. Look for the salvation of the Lord.
question: Where do you feel trapped today, and how could you stand still and watch for God to make a way?
prayer: Lord, when I feel trapped with nowhere to turn, help me stand still and see Your salvation. You made a way through the sea, and You can make a way for me. Amen.

text: The LORD shall fight for you, and ye shall hold your peace.
reflection: Moses continued his words to the frightened Israelites with a promise: "The LORD shall fight for you, and ye shall hold your peace." Hold your peace means be quiet, be calm. The people had been crying out in fear and complaint. Moses told them their part now was to be still and let God act. There is great comfort in this. We are not left to defend ourselves against every enemy. God steps in on our behalf. He is a warrior for His people. Some of our battles are against people. Others are against fears, temptations, or circumstances. In each case, there is a place for doing what we can. But there is also a place for quiet trust, for letting God handle what is beyond us. Holding our peace may mean not answering every criticism, not taking revenge, or not trying to control every outcome. Today, rest in this promise. The Lord shall fight for you. You can hold your peace.
question: What fight could you stop striving in today and trust the Lord to fight for you?
prayer: Lord, You shall fight for me, and I shall hold my peace. Calm my anxious striving, and let me rest in Your promise to step in for me today. Amen.

text: The LORD is on my side; I will not fear: what can man do unto me?
reflection: Psalm 118 is a song of victory sung by someone who had been surrounded by enemies. In the middle of it comes a confident declaration: "The LORD is on my side; I will not fear: what can man do unto me?" This is not arrogance. The psalmist is not saying people cannot hurt him. He had clearly been threatened. He is saying that with God on his side, no human power has the final word. People can criticize, oppose, or mistreat us. They can make life difficult. But they cannot undo God's love, cancel His promises, or remove us from His care. When we know the Lord is on our side, the opinions and threats of others lose their power to control us. Fear of people is a heavy burden. It makes us anxious, timid, and eager to please. Today, if someone's opinion or opposition is weighing on you, remember who is on your side. Let that truth set you free from fear.
question: Whose opinion or opposition have you been fearing, and how does knowing God is on your side change that?
prayer: Lord, You are on my side, and I will not fear what people can do to me. Free me from the fear of others, and let me rest secure in Your love. Amen.

text: And we know that all things work together for good to them that love God, to them who are the called according to his purpose.
reflection: Romans 8:28 is a verse that is quoted again and again, and also one of the most misunderstood: "And we know that all things work together for good to them that love God, to them who are the called according to his purpose." It does not say all things are good. Some things that happen to us are painful and wrong. It says all things work together for good. Like ingredients in a recipe, some of which taste bitter alone, God weaves even hard things into His good purpose. Notice also who this promise is for: those who love God and are called according to His purpose. And notice what good means. The next verse explains that God's purpose is to make us like His Son. The good He is working toward is not always comfort, but Christlikeness. If you are in a painful season, you may not see the good yet. But you can trust that God is weaving it together. Nothing is wasted in His hands.
question: What hard thing could you trust God to weave into His good purpose?
prayer: Lord, I know that all things work together for good to them that love You. I do not see how yet, but I trust that nothing is wasted in Your hands. Amen.

text: What shall we then say to these things? If God be for us, who can be against us?
reflection: After describing God's purpose to make us like His Son, Paul asks a question: "What shall we then say to these things? If God be for us, who can be against us?" It is not that no one will ever oppose us. Paul faced plenty of opposition. It is that no opposition can ultimately succeed against those whom God is for. And how do we know God is for us? Paul answers in the very next verse. He did not spare His own Son but gave Him up for us all. If God has already given the greatest gift, will He not also give us everything else we truly need? God being for us is not a vague hope. It is proven by what He has already done. When you feel outnumbered, overwhelmed, or condemned, remember this question. Who can be against you? Not circumstances, not accusers, not even your own failures. God is for you, and that changes everything.
question: Where do you feel outnumbered, and how does God's gift of His Son prove He is for you?
prayer: Father, if You are for me, who can be against me? You did not spare Your own Son. When I feel outnumbered, remind me that You are on my side. Amen.

text: And he answered, Fear not: for they that be with us are more than they that be with them.
reflection: The king of Syria sent an army to capture the prophet Elisha. In the morning, Elisha's servant woke to see the city surrounded by horses and chariots. Terrified, he cried, Alas, my master! What shall we do? Elisha's response was calm: "Fear not: for they that be with us are more than they that be with them." The servant must have looked around in confusion. He saw only two of them against an army. Then Elisha prayed that God would open his servant's eyes. Suddenly the young man saw the mountain full of horses and chariots of fire surrounding Elisha. God's army had been there all along. He just could not see it. Our eyes often see only the threat. We count the enemies and the problems and feel hopelessly outnumbered. But there is more going on than we can see. God's protection is real, even when it is invisible. Pray today that God would open your eyes to His presence and power around you.
question: Where do you need God to open your eyes to His presence around you today?
prayer: Lord, open my eyes as You opened the eyes of Elisha's servant. Let me see that those who are with me are more than those who are against me. Amen.

text: My help cometh from the LORD, which made heaven and earth.
reflection: Psalm 121 was sung by pilgrims travelling to Jerusalem. As they walked, they would see the hills ahead, perhaps beautiful, perhaps hiding dangers. The psalm begins by lifting the eyes to the hills and asking where help comes from. Then it answers: "My help cometh from the LORD, which made heaven and earth." Help does not come from the hills themselves, or from anything else in creation. It comes from the Creator. The One who made heaven and earth is the One who helps us. That description is important. If God made everything, then nothing is beyond His power. No problem is too big for the Maker of the universe. The rest of the psalm describes a God who never sleeps, who watches over our coming and going, and who keeps us from harm. Where are you looking for help today? Look past the hills, past the people, past the plans. Look to the Lord who made heaven and earth.
question: What lesser source of help have you been leaning on, and how could you look to the Lord instead?
prayer: Lord, my help comes from You, the Maker of heaven and earth. Nothing is too hard for You. Turn my eyes from lesser helps to You today. Amen.

text: Blessed is the man that trusteth in the LORD, and whose hope the LORD is.
reflection: Jeremiah 17 sets two kinds of people side by side. The first trusts in people and makes flesh his strength. He is like a shrub in the desert, dry and lifeless. But the second is different: "Blessed is the man that trusteth in the LORD, and whose hope the LORD is." Notice the double emphasis. This person trusts in the Lord, and the Lord is his hope. Not just someone he hopes in, but his hope itself. Everything rests on God. This is a choice we make many times each day. When worries arise, we can lean on our own plans, other people's approval, money, or our abilities. Or we can lean on God. Human help is not wrong. God often works through people. But when our ultimate trust rests on anything other than Him, we end up dry. The blessed life is not necessarily the easy life. It is the life rooted in God. Make Him your trust and your hope today.
question: Where does your confidence really rest right now, in people or in the Lord?
prayer: Lord, blessed is the one who trusts in You and whose hope You are. Where I have relied on anything else, turn my trust back to You today. Amen.

text: For he shall be as a tree planted by the waters, and that spreadeth out her roots by the river, and shall not see when heat cometh, but her leaf shall be green; and shall not be careful in the year of drought, neither shall cease from yielding fruit.
reflection: Jeremiah continues with a beautiful picture of the person who trusts in God: "he shall be as a tree planted by the waters, and that spreadeth out her roots by the river, and shall not see when heat cometh, but her leaf shall be green." Picture a tree growing beside a river. Its roots go deep, drawing water from a constant source. When the heat comes, it does not wither. When drought strikes, it keeps producing fruit. The heat still comes, and the drought still arrives. The tree is not spared hard seasons. But it is not destroyed by them, because its roots reach a source the drought cannot dry up. This is what trusting God does for us. It does not exempt us from trouble, but it keeps us green and fruitful in the middle of it. Our roots reach God Himself. Today, push your roots deeper. Spend time in His Word and in prayer. Draw from the river that never runs dry.
question: How could you push your roots deeper into God during this season?
prayer: Lord, make me like a tree planted by the waters, green and fruitful even in drought. Draw my roots deeper into You, so I do not wither when the heat comes. Amen.

text: Let not your heart be troubled: ye believe in God, believe also in me.
reflection: Jesus spoke these words to His disciples when their hearts were heavy. He had been telling them that He would soon go away, and they were confused and afraid. So He said, "Let not your heart be troubled: ye believe in God, believe also in me." Notice that Jesus treats a troubled heart as something we have some say over. Let not means do not allow it. We cannot always control what happens around us, but we can choose where we turn our trust. And Jesus gives the remedy: believe. Trust God, and trust Jesus. He does not say the situation is not serious. He says there is Someone more powerful than the situation. A troubled heart is often a heart that has forgotten who is in control. Faith reminds it. What is troubling your heart today? Name it. Then bring it to Jesus. Choose, as an act of faith, not to let it rule you. Believe in God, and believe also in Him.
question: What is troubling your heart today, and could you name it and bring it to Jesus?
prayer: Lord Jesus, You tell me not to let my heart be troubled. I believe in God, and I believe in You. I bring You what troubles me and rest my heart in You. Amen.

text: Some trust in chariots, and some in horses: but we will remember the name of the LORD our God.
reflection: In ancient warfare, chariots and horses were the most advanced military technology. A nation with many chariots felt secure. But David wrote, "Some trust in chariots, and some in horses: but we will remember the name of the LORD our God." Everyone trusts in something. Today our chariots and horses might be bank accounts, careers, health, education, or connections. None of these are bad. But they are poor places to rest our ultimate confidence. They can fail. Markets fall, jobs end, and health declines. David chose to remember the name of the Lord. Remembering is an act of faith. It means calling to mind who God is and what He has done. His name stands for His character, His faithfulness, His power, and His love. As March comes to a close, consider where your confidence truly rests. Thank God for the good things He has given you. But place your trust in His name above them all.
question: What chariots and horses are you tempted to trust in, and how could you place your confidence in God?
prayer: Lord, some trust in chariots and some in horses, but I will remember Your name. Only You never fail. I place my confidence in You today. Amen.
